title: How Code in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Becomes Write-Only and Disposable
gist: Reporting on Phillip Mortimer's QCon London talk, Ben Linders covers the argument that AI-generated code is inherently write-only and disposable — too dense to read, defined instead by its tests, better rewritten than debugged, and unreviewable by humans at scale — pushing organizations toward automated review, self-healing software, and creativity as the developer's remaining differentiated value.

insights.claim: Phillip Mortimer argues AI makes all code effectively write-only — too dense to read directly — so the only practical way to understand what such code does is through extensive test cases, which become the code's documentation, citing Eric S. Raymond's original definition of write-only code.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Reframes code-quality practice: if reading code stops being the verification method, teams should invest in comprehensive test suites as the primary spec and audit trail rather than code readability standards.
insights.quote: When you write code that is too dense to read, the only way to understand what it does is through extensive test cases. The tests become the documentation for your code.
insights.locator: A principle to deal with such code is that the tests define the behaviour

insights.claim: Mortimer frames write-only code as not a new phenomenon — languages like APL and regular expressions have always traded readability for density and power — and positions AI-generated code as exhibiting the same trade-off, just applied at much larger scale.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Gives a historical precedent for evaluating whether write-only AI code is manageable: teams that already tolerate APL/regex-style density have existing practices (tests-as-spec) that transfer directly.
insights.locator: Certain languages are write-only by design

insights.claim: Mortimer argues generated code should be treated as disposable rather than debugged: because write-only code is hard to fix, it is often faster to keep the test suite and rewrite the implementation from scratch than to modify what already exists.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Challenges the default engineering instinct to patch existing code — for AI-generated code, budgeting for rewrite-over-debug may be the faster and cheaper default.
insights.quote: Write-only code is so hard to debug. It’s often easier to rewrite the code from scratch than it is to modify what you’ve already written.
insights.locator: Another principle Mortimer mentioned was that the code is disposable

insights.claim: Mortimer argues line-by-line human review of AI-generated code does not scale because humans quickly become the bottleneck, making automated review a necessity rather than an optimization once AI-generated code volume rises.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A direct argument for investing in automated code-review tooling now, before human review capacity becomes the binding constraint on shipping velocity.
insights.quote: There’s no point in having humans try to review AI-generated code line by line, because humans very quickly become the bottleneck.
insights.locator: Humans can’t review generated code due to the sheer volume

insights.claim: Mortimer's proposed mechanism for automated review is a coding-agent harness invoked as a CI action, running a skill that encodes what a senior developer would look for, able to post comments, request changes, or approve a pull request directly.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: A concrete, implementable pattern — CI-invoked review agent with a codified senior-dev skill — that engineering teams can adopt as a first step toward automated review.
insights.locator: This is relatively straightforward - a coding agent harness can be invoked as a CI action

insights.claim: Contrary to the intuition that a model reviewing its own output would be weak, Mortimer reports seeing many cases where a different prompt, instruction set, and context produced genuinely valuable review comments that caught bugs before deployment, and frames this adversarial self-review pattern as an increasingly common technique across agentic systems generally, not just code review.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Suggests 'self-review with a different context' is a viable, low-cost technique worth testing before investing in a separate review model or vendor.
insights.quote: You might think that having a model review its own output would be ineffective - but I’ve seen many examples of this process providing really valuable review comments, catching bugs before they get deployed.
insights.locator: InfoQ: How can we automate code reviews?

insights.claim: Mortimer recommends running 'de-slopify' agents on a regular cadence outside the pull-request loop against the whole codebase, to catch structural issues a single-PR review would miss, such as repeated code, unparameterized tests, and unused feature flags.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Identifies a review gap (structural/cross-file issues invisible to per-PR review) as a distinct, addressable product and process category.
insights.locator: Code review agents can also be set up to run outside of the pull request loop

insights.claim: Mortimer suggests software should increasingly heal itself: an AI coding agent listening to an observability platform, aggregating alerts over a time window, and automatically raising pull requests to fix the most commonly recurring problems first.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Points to observability-to-remediation automation as an emerging workflow, relevant for teams evaluating AIOps/incident-response tooling investment.
insights.quote: A powerful thing to do is to have an AI coding agent listen to your observability platform, aggregate alerts over some time window, and start raising pull requests to fix the problems that it’s seen, starting with the most common ones.
insights.locator: He also suggested that software should heal itself

insights.claim: Mortimer argues AI is decoupling developer intent from implementation because natural-language-driven coding makes developers portable across programming languages, effectively making every developer a full-stack developer regardless of prior language specialization.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Implies language-specialization as a hiring or career differentiator weakens as AI coding tools mature, shifting evaluation toward problem-framing and creative ability instead.
insights.quote: We are all full stack developers; all you need is a creative idea
insights.locator: And there’s never been a better time to build with software than today

themes.theme: Creativity as the developer's remaining differentiator

insights.claim: With AI framed as having solved the implementation problem, Mortimer argues the developer's remaining differentiated value is creativity — iterative, step-by-step improvement compounded over long periods, not a single flash of insight.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Reframes what skills to hire for and train as AI absorbs implementation work: sustained iterative problem-solving over raw coding output.
insights.quote: Creativity is iterative. It’s step-by-step improvement over long periods of time. Anyone can create. You just need to start working.
insights.locator: The role for the software developer today is creativity

insights.claim: Mortimer recommends organizations protect uninterrupted focus time by clustering meetings at the start or end of the day, since creative people often work best alone — citing that brainstorming, a favored corporate technique, has been shown to produce fewer good ideas than individuals working independently.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: An actionable org-design change (calendar structure over group-brainstorm rituals) for engineering leaders trying to increase creative output as AI absorbs routine implementation.
insights.locator: Creative people need time and space to work

insights.claim: Mortimer points to constraints as a creativity forcing function, citing his own experience at document-intelligence startup Accelex, where early-stage time and resource constraints forced innovative solutions to the problem of reading data out of tables.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Suggests resource-constrained teams may out-innovate well-funded ones on specific hard subproblems, relevant context when evaluating early-stage document-intelligence or data-extraction startups.
insights.locator: Constraints are also important in creative work

insights.claim: Mortimer warns that the drive for 'hyper-velocity engineering' enabled by AI leaves less time to pause and reflect, making protected time and space for creative thinking more important now than ever, not less.
insights.speaker: Ben Linders
insights.so_what: Cautions against treating AI-driven speed gains as a reason to compress reflection time — the opposite may better sustain creative output.
insights.locator: as the drive for hyper-velocity engineering leaves less and less time to pause
